articles.title: West Point’s Honor Code Taught the Military to Lie
articles.author: Jasper Craven
articles.content: On May 12, 1962, General Douglas MacArthur strode into the West Point mess hall and delivered a stirring farewell address before an audience of more than two thousand cadets. It had been just over a year since another famed former general, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, had famously delivered his own closing warning about industry’s capture of the Pentagon. Now MacArthur seemed worried about the corruption of the American soldier’s soul — the death of honor itself. Honor was everything to MacArthur. Between 1919 and 1922, as West Point superintendent, he built cadet life around the academy’s hallowed motto, “Duty, Honor, Country.” He further instituted a cadet honor code and attendant honor boards, a quasi-judicial trial system meant to discourage unethical behavior and promote a culture of leadership among fledgling recruits. While honor is traditionally equated with honesty, integrity, and accountability, it doesn’t require any of these things by definition. Rather, it denotes fidelity to an institution’s core rites and standards, making it a fragile, fungible concept whose strictures shift depending on who is giving the orders. In the mess hall that day, MacArthur conjured honor in its purest form, urging the sea of cadets before him “to learn to stand up in the storm, but to have compassion on those who fall; to master yourself before you seek to master others; to have a heart that is clean, a goal that is high.” He called upon them “to be modest so that you will remember the simplicity of true greatness, the open mind of true wisdom, the meekness of true strength.” MacArthur was a fearsome figure, but like any good military mind, he knew the importance of building soldiers with camaraderie, humility, and intelligence. In his stint as West Point superintendent, MacArthur cut down on hazing and expanded academic freedom. He took the education of these warriors in training seriously, even fortifying the humanities as a critical part of their moral development. For the first time, he provided cadets with access to the daily newspapers, a policy that was viciously opposed by a cadre of influential graduates who prized West Point’s insularity. After just three years on the job, that influential cadre, now ensconced in the War Department, transferred MacArthur to the Philippines and reversed his dictate. MacArthur’s ideal of the honorable, well-read, and well-rounded officer was an inspiring conception of service but one that would soon come under grave threat from West Point’s superintendent, William Westmoreland, who, a year after MacArthur’s speech, departed the school to run a campaign in Vietnam racked by war crimes, cooked books, and countless strategic failures. During a sojourn to MacArthur’s apartment at the Waldorf Astoria just before this appointment, the wizened general told Westmoreland that the war in southeast Asia was “fraught with hazards” and could only be won with a “scorched earth policy.” Despite Westmoreland’s profound shortcomings and corruption, he, like many other military architects in Vietnam, would retire in good standing, his reputation helpfully revised via a fawning biography written by West Point’s chair of American history. As the war corroded both honesty and integrity throughout the ranks, heady notions like honor were reduced to meaningless platitudes. President Richard Nixon frequently invoked the vagaries of honor to mask Vietnam’s discredited premise and the degenerate killing that proliferated. When, on January 23, 1973, Nixon announced the end of the war in a short but defiant speech, he used the phrase “peace with honor” five times. The same year as Nixon’s speech, Captain Michael Rose, a young Air Force Academy graduate studying at New York University Law School, published A Prayer for Relief , a damning 253-page investigation into the dysfunctions of MacArthur’s beloved Cadet Honor Code. Over months, Rose collected interviews and intelligence from major training grounds for future military brass, among them all five service academies, including West Point and the Air Force Academy, plus the Virginia Military Institute and the Citadel. His inquiry was powerfully cosigned by a contingent of federal lawmakers, who explicitly counseled military schools to accommodate Rose’s requests for access. They did so begrudgingly, especially at West Point, which actively frustrated his efforts. “The military police there were following me,” he said. West Point also refused to connect Rose to James Pelosi, a cadet then facing a gauntlet of hazing for failing to immediately put down his pencil at the conclusion of a test. Rose ultimately managed to sneak into West Point’s Camp Buckner, a training facility a few miles from the academy on Lake Popolopen, where he went tent to tent one night looking for Pelosi until he found him. “Then he and I went into the latrine, and I tape-recorded him for an hour.” Pelosi’s assessment of military honor was unsparing. “I’m disillusioned with the air of elitism, of perfection, around here,” he said. “People think that just by being here they’re automatically a little bit better than anyone else. But they’re not.” Rose’s resulting thesis was simple but devastating: the military’s festering morality crisis — evidenced by “pandemic drug addiction, racial tension, sedition, common crime, refusal of combat duty, widespread assaults and murders of officers [and] rapidly increasing desertion and decreasing reenlistments” — could be traced back to the transactional notions of honor perpetrated at places like West Point. His argument was crafted from a powerful combination of legalistic analysis and hundreds of vivid interviews from sources sketching out scenes that often seemed plucked from a hard-boiled police drama. Rose documented tainted honor board investigations and corrupt cadet interrogators, some of whom turned off their tape recorders to scream threats at defendants, forcibly cut their hair, and deprive them of sleep. One cadet said the pressure became so bad that he vomited. Others compared the experience to the mock prisoner-of-war interrogation training that school officials had instituted a few months earlier. Honor-code-related punishments were often biased and freighted with personal baggage. The chairman of one honor board stated his hostility toward a cadet on trial. “This guy has been in trouble before,” he said. “And we don’t want that kind around.” Cadets, many of them under twenty-one, who sought to appeal their honor board decisions were often threatened with a more serious military court-martial, which, due to the military justice system’s punishing and capricious nature, could entail imprisonment at Fort Leavenworth. Prosecution could stem from any number of offenses. Hundreds of regulations dictating cadet life were itemized in a standard-issue manual known as the Blue Book. Infractions were often vague, making them easily exploitable. They included “general inattention,” “carelessness,” and exercising “poor judgment.” Cadets were technically considered in violation of the honor code for asking a fellow cadet how to spell a word for an essay assignment, or for telling a fib. One cadet who told a superior he had done twenty push-ups when, in fact, he had done eighteen had the book thrown at him. Another who lied about shaving was expelled. Admitting one’s failings could also end in expulsion. “The code,” one West Pointer griped, “weeds out some cadets who are honest enough to report themselves for honor violations.” Even cadets who reported others for wrongdoing were sometimes expelled for “tolerating” bad behavior, imparting what some administrators quietly worried was a warped lesson, namely that “those who said ‘no comment’ or lied fared better than those who told the truth.” One West Point professor argued that these “seemingly purposeless rules breed resentment,” which in turn curdles into a full-blown rejection of morality. The honor code was a stand-in for respectable behavior, and yet cadets found it nearly impossible to stay in the code’s good graces. It could be fairly reasoned from here that the code was simply too rigid and that rule-breaking was the only way to survive. “Cadets,” Rose’s report concluded, “learn by example that deceit and deception are ‘standard operating procedure’ when the image of West Point or the Army is at stake.” His assertion was backed up by scores of cadets and even in-house psychiatrists. “I hear leaders talking about integrity and spirit and intent,” confessed one cadet. “But I see few who live by their preaching.” MacArthur’s high-minded crusade a generation earlier had led to something far more brutal and duplicitous than the “Athens on the Hudson” he had prescribed. As one commentator argued in Time magazine, the new batch of senior military leaders tasked with teaching ethics had become infamous for “falsifying body counts, concealing the bombing of Cambodia, [and] covering up My Lai.” At this time, West Point offered a single ethics course, an elective that was only available senior year. By the Vietnam War’s end , few cadets held MacArthurian feelings about honor. Sixty percent of West Point cadets, for instance, asserted in a 1974 survey that “adherence to the spirit of the Honor Code is deteriorating.” This, according to an accompanying study, could be traced back to the military’s “sanctimonious” belief in honor, which obscured the true knottiness of ethics. This was a generational loss of military integrity, and yet because it largely played out in academic environments, it often took the form of seemingly insignificant cheating rings. A series of major cheating scandals broke out at the service academies during the Cold War: in 1951, in 1967, in 1972, and then, not long after the fall of Saigon , in 1976. Air Force Academy Dean Robert McDermott defensively blamed the 1967 scandal on civilian counterculture, testifying to congressional investigators that dozens of identified cheaters had hailed from a clique “symbolized by kooky music, long hair, and a few other things.” A subsequent report penned by a committee of retired brass and academics disagreed, blaming the behavior on an academic environment concerned with “the symbols of achievement, sometimes at the expense of reality.” This shift in military culture was impossibly swift, evident in the case of West Point cadet Joseph Zengerle, whose hopes were high when, as a first-year plebe, he marched at John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inauguration. He absorbed, in person, Kennedy’s rousing call to “ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.” Months later, he was there in the mess hall for General MacArthur’s humanistic farewell address. And yet shortly before his graduation from West Point, Zengerle marched at Kennedy’s funeral. The event presaged a darker politics and the continuation of a poisonous war, things that the man in the casket had tried to curb. Soon after, Zengerle was sent to Vietnam to be Westmoreland’s aide-de-camp. Rose’s report, meanwhile, was ignored, and the Air Force’s judge advocate general declined to certify him as a military lawyer. By the summer of 1974, brass had coerced him to resign. The deep issues Rose spotlighted continued bubbling up to the surface, often in the form of schoolyard deceptions. In 1976, more than 150 West Point cadets were charged with cheating, this time within the academy’s most storied and prestigious department: electrical engineering. Some assessments later indicated that as many as six hundred cadets had cheated, but even the smaller statistic qualified the 1976 affair as the worst cheating scandal in military history. One of the many cadets forced to resign was Robert K. Koster, son of Samuel Koster, an Army officer who helped cover up My Lai and previously ran West Point. After the war, many in the Pentagon fell victim to ego, blinkeredness, and historical revisionism. There was no reckoning with the war’s failures. This avoidance was typified by the POW-MIA movement, which, according to historian Rick Perlstein, was used “to justify the carnage in Vietnam in a way that rendered the United States as its sole victim.” Vietnam, along with the civil rights movement, saw the inflammation of the “Lost Cause” myth around the Civil War, manifested when President Nixon attempted to erect a monument to the Confederacy on West Point’s grounds. Today the warped lessons of the “Lost Cause” and POW-MIA continue to be nurtured by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , who has himself introduced a new fiction for his generation, namely that DEI was the major cause for America’s losses in Iraq and Afghanistan. Like MacArthur, Hegseth has made his own rhetorical paeans to honor, writing in his 2024 book The War on Warriors that it was a cornerstone commandment of “America’s civil religion.” By his definition, honor is for those with high casualty counts and reactionary politics. He wrote that honor was under threat from leftist causes, among them: “Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI), Critical Race Theory (CRT), feminism, genderism, safetyism, climate worship, manufactured ‘violent extremism,’ straight-up weirdo shit, and a grab bag of social justice causes.” Still, in a few fleeting paragraphs, Hegseth offers a cogent analysis of the rot, eloquently fusing MacArthur’s worries about military honesty with Eisenhower’s warnings about military spending. “Once you pin a star on your shoulder, the political pressure mounts,” Hegseth wrote. “Go-along-to-get-along, and get promoted, is the smoothest path. Don’t rock the boat, do what your political masters tell you, never admit mistakes — and get promoted. Then, once you retire, you get to collect a pension and a sweet job from Lockheed Martin.” In these pages, Hegseth proclaims that American generals should be statutorily restricted from comfortably migrating from their “comfy desk jobs in the Pentagon to the boardroom of the military-industrial complex.” It was a veiled swipe, perhaps, at President Joe Biden’s defense secretary, Lloyd Austin, who left a seat on Raytheon’s board to become the first black American to hold the position. A few months after his book was published, in November 2024, Hegseth was himself unexpectedly nominated to run the Pentagon. During his confirmation hearings, he sketched out how he would construct a hard-charging, unrepentantly violent, and blatantly ahistorical Department of War — departments of mere “defense” were no longer up to the task. In a flash, he dropped any of his past diagnoses about the Pentagon’s true problems, instead hypercharging all the agency’s worst qualities. Hegseth pushed the Pentagon budget past $1 trillion, retaliated against brass simply for their gender or skin color, engaged in war crimes, and prioritized his own future and personal vanity above all else, installing a makeup studio at the Pentagon and having government employees film his workouts and upload them to social media. Hegseth also barred from the Pentagon briefing room photographers who took unflattering photos of him. At one point during his confirmation hearing, US Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed Hegseth on his shifting stance regarding the dangers of military-industrial influence. “You’re quite sure that every general who serves should not go directly into the defense industry for ten years, but you’re not willing to make that same pledge?” she pressed. Hegseth smirked. “I’m not a general, Senator,” he said. One of the first things Hegseth did once in office was to crack down on academic freedom at places like West Point, banning books, pushing out professors, and reinterpreting the honor code. In a strange twist, a major ally in his fight is Michael Rose, who, under Biden, became a fierce critic of DEI policies and COVID-19 mandates. In little more than a year, Hegseth has done much damage, though the culture of the US Armed Forces was deeply compromised decades ago. For years, a certain subset of cadets has come to see deception as an ingrained part of military life, represented by a circulating joke about West Point’s motto that goes “Duty, Country, Hon — well, two out of three ain’t bad.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Paging Hezbollah? Exposing Israel’s terrorist pager attack on Lebanon | w/ Radwan Mortada
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Two years after Israel’s pager attacks on Lebanon killed dozens and maimed thousands, Lebanese investigative journalist Radwan Mortada’s new two-part Al Jazeera documentary, The Trap (Al-Mesyada), goes inside the September 2024 Mossad operation more than a decade in the making. Mortada joins Rania Khalek to trace the web of front companies stretching from Taiwan to Bulgaria that enabled Israel to infiltrate Gold Apollo, a supplier Hezbollah had trusted for decades. As a new Israeli propaganda film Paging Hezbollah heads for US theaters, Mortada reveals that Israel’s goal to kill as many as 20,000 Hezbollah fighters with booby-trapped walkie-talkies, in fact, fell far short. He also breaks down Hezbollah’s own fatal mistakes, and the lasting psychological toll of a terrorist attack that, contrary to US and Israeli narratives, was far from “precise” or “targeted,” destroying the lives of children, families, and medical workers. “Hezbollah’s biggest mistake was forgetting Israel’s capabilities – forgetting how bloody and cruel they can be.” Watch The Trap Part 1: aljazeera360.com/video/1017661 Part 2: aljazeera360.com/video/1017626 Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! ****** Rough transcript follows: [Rana:] And joining me to discuss this two-part investigative deep dive into the pager attacks is the producer himself, Redwan Mortada. Redwan, welcome to Breakthrough News Live. [Redwan Mortada:] Thank you, Rana. Thank you for having me. [Rana:] Well, it’s a real pleasure, and I got a chance to watch the documentary. I encourage everybody to go check it out. It’s available online. It’s also available with English subtitles, and it’s really worth the watch. I mean, you expose so much new information we didn’t know before. But before we get into some of the specifics, Redwan, I want to ask you, you’ve called this one of the most complex cases that you’ve ever worked on as an investigative journalist. And we have all watched Israel commit so many atrocities across Lebanon that have killed far more people than the pager attacks did. Yet, in your film, you call this the most devastating blow that Hezbollah has taken since its founding. So, two years on from this attack, why does this operation still loom so large that you felt it warranted a two-part investigative series? [Redwan Mortada:] You’re right, Rania. Israel killed tens of thousands of Lebanese over the years. But in fact, this operation is different—the pager attack. I mean, because it came from a place Hezbollah thought was secure for years and years, for decades, if you want. There has been an intelligence war between the resistance, mainly between Hezbollah and Israel, in Lebanon and in the region. Israel assassinated several senior commanders of Hezbollah, carried out several operations against it, killing Abbas al-Musawi, the ex-secretary-general, and at the same time, Hezbollah carried out several operations against Israel. But this pager operation was different because it was one of the biggest blows to Hezbollah—an attack that only Mossad could imagine. No one could imagine this kind of operation and this kind of killing, because it didn’t only affect Hezbollah fighters. It affected tons of children and women, and it breaches all international and humanitarian rules across the world. [Rana:] Yeah. And just for everybody who’s watching Breakthrough News and your organization, Blue House Films, you produced a documentary on the pager attacks and how they impacted civilians specifically that came out last year. People who are probably watching this have seen that documentary, and it shows the toll specifically on children and other civilians caught up in it—their faces totally maimed, destroyed, and blinded for those who did survive. I mean, just a horrific attack. But your documentary, this two-part series, really dives deep into the timeline of Israel plotting this attack. I mean, Israel spent years on this; it started back in 2015. And in your documentary, you lay out how Mossad built these front companies spanning Taiwan, Hong Kong, Hungary, and Bulgaria. They infiltrated the pager company that Hezbollah had grown to trust, they manipulated the Hezbollah representative that was dealing with that company, and they rigged the devices with small amounts of this powerful explosive substance hidden in the batteries that was so hard to detect, and then they detonated them at a moment of their choosing. I mean, the way you lay it out, it plays like a movie thriller. So walk us through some of that Israeli timeline—how did they pull this off? [Redwan Mortada:] It is a long story. You have to watch the film and go deep into the details, the exclusive information, the exclusive data, and the interviews, because it also presents the story of Hezbollah. We post in the film the email communications between the company called Gold Apollo and Hezbollah. But in fact, if I want to go back to how this started, after the 2006 war, Israel started looking for ways to penetrate Hezbollah, especially its network and communication, because you know the result of the war in 2006 was that Hezbollah beat Israel, and Israel wanted revenge. So they started trying to penetrate Hezbollah. They tried to recruit the sales representatives in Taiwan; they failed. They tried to sell pagers to Hezbollah through several front companies, but they failed. And the story they distributed in the media about a blonde girl that manipulated a representative to sell him the pagers was not true. The truth is that they penetrated a trusted company that had a relation with this company over 20 years, starting in the 2000s—Gold Apollo. So they penetrated Hezbollah through this company. They recruited Teresa, the employee in the company, and through recruiting Teresa, they penetrated Hezbollah, and they sent these pagers. And it was not just one plan for Mossad; there was a Plan A and a Plan B. Plan A was to explode the walkie-talkies, and this operation started in 2014. I am not saying that Israeli officials declared that, but they succeeded in sending 15,000 walkie-talkies to Hezbollah. But these walkie-talkies were in storage, and Hezbollah did not decide to go into battle in full power, so they did not distribute all the walkie-talkies; they distributed around 800 walkie-talkies. So Mossad moved to the second plan, which is Plan B—detonating the pagers. This operation started in 2020, and they succeeded in sending 500 pagers to Hezbollah at the beginning, in 2023. Because of the necessity of the battle at the beginning, Hezbollah refused these pagers because this model—the new model—was different; he had ordered the old model. Gold Apollo sent Hezbollah the new model, and the representative of Hezbollah whose name was Mike said, “We don’t want to deal with you because we ordered the old version.” But because of the necessity of the battle and the urge of what was going on after October 7, it forced Hezbollah to receive 4,200 pagers, and they distributed around 3,000, of which only 1,850 exploded. [Rana:] Yeah. And people really need to go watch this documentary, because you also lay out how the Israelis would find out that Hezbollah was on to them, and then they would stop scanners from Iran from coming to Lebanon that could have detected the substance by bombing a warehouse and another warehouse, and then claiming they were bombing this to kill somebody when it was really to stop Hezbollah from finding out about the pagers. I mean, it’s just really wild stuff. But I want to talk about Hezbollah’s mistakes here, because the attack did expose how deeply Hezbollah had been penetrated, which is what you’re talking about. And you mentioned 2006. After 2006, Hezbollah did build its own communications network, and you described in the documentary how this is precisely because Lebanon’s telecoms were so compromised by the Israelis. And then the war in Syria turned Hezbollah into a much larger and more exposed army that allowed for more penetration. At the same time, these failures come off as so shocking, because Hezbollah did have guardrails in place to try to detect if anything was messed with. What were some of Hezbollah’s mistakes? Again, people really should go watch the documentary because you go into deep detail on what those mistakes were. But if you had to give a brief explanation, what were Hezbollah’s mistakes, and could this have been prevented? And I guess I’d also add to that, has Hezbollah reckoned with this internally? [Redwan Mortada:] I said it in the film, and I will repeat it: the biggest mistake was forgetting Israeli capabilities and forgetting how bloody and cruel they can be. This is one of the biggest mistakes Hezbollah committed. In fact, you’re right, the war in Syria exposed Hezbollah, and the capabilities and advanced technology Israel had also helped them to do this operation. But in addition to that, they used a new kind of technology, which is CL-20—a new kind of US explosive material manufactured by the United States of America. This kind of explosion is not detectable, and also when Hezbollah gave the pagers that did not explode to the Lebanese army, when they detected it… I put in the film that report that mentions this is an unknown material; it’s not listed in the explosive library. That’s why the airport scanners in Hong Kong, Turkey, and Lebanon couldn’t detect it. [Rana:] That’s so scary. It’s so scary to think what else they’ve infiltrated. [Redwan Mortada:] Especially, Rana, these pager devices are civilian devices; they are not military devices. [Rana:] Yeah. Well, you also—I thought it was super interesting—mentioned in the documentary that Hezbollah’s Imad Mughniyeh used to cut open screws when he would take apart devices to make sure the screw hadn’t been messed with. I mean, one of the biggest mistakes that was mentioned was that Hezbollah operatives were asking questions—there was something weird about these pagers and walkie-talkies, and they were taking them apart and looking at the different pieces to see what was wrong with them, but they never cut open the batteries because… [Redwan Mortada:] Okay, that shows a lot, by the way. That shows a lot, because even us at the time, when this happened, our question was: where was Hezbollah? Where was the protocol for experimenting on all of these? In fact, I mentioned in the film that there was like a mind race between Hezbollah and the Mossad officer, and it was one step… I mentioned two names in the film, and Jibril Jibril is a nickname for Hussein Bazi, an engineer inside Hezbollah. He was an officer who had doubts, and when he started to remove these pagers from small groups, Israel knew about that and decided to start the operation instead of losing the element of surprise. [Rana:] So that they could do at least some damage, even though they didn’t get to kill as many people as they wanted. I wanted to ask you, though, obviously this did not destroy Hezbollah because they were able to go on and fight the war in 2024, but it did do a lot of damage to the organization. So can you explain, in terms of manpower, command, morale, and trust in their own systems, what was the damage of this operation to Hezbollah? [Redwan Mortada:] For me, I think the biggest impact was psychological. The Israelis started this war by exploding the pagers. The first day they exploded the pagers; the second day they exploded the walkie-talkies. Then they carried out over 1,400 airstrikes on Lebanon in one day. After that, they assassinated the special forces commanders—the Radwan Force in Hezbollah—until they assassinated Hassan Nasrallah. For around 10 days, Hezbollah and Lebanese society experienced and went through one of the hardest days in our history. The goal and target for Israel was to destroy Hezbollah. But in fact, Hezbollah survived, and you can tell that if you do a comparison between the war in 2024 and the war in 2026, the level of assassination and the level of penetration wasn’t the same at all. [Rana:] I want to ask you also, Redwan, you talked about this in your documentary, and I covered it in the documentary that I did with Blue House: Israel and its supporters continue to celebrate this as a marvel of precision. They call it surgical, targeted, and clean. And actually, I don’t know if you’ve seen, but the Israelis also have a movie coming out called Paging Hezbollah. [Redwan Mortada:] A propaganda film, you mean? The propaganda film where they started swimming and they are at the beach, and you will hear another voice: “We are in a special area, but in fact, we are in a hostile environment where everyone wants to destroy us”? They are justifying why they went into a major operation. [Rana:] Yeah. So this is going to be in American theaters on October 30th. It’s called Paging Hezbollah, an Israeli propaganda film that celebrates this attack. I encourage people, instead of watching that, to go watch Redwan’s documentary, which we’ll include a link to in the description. But I wanted to ask you, what was the actual impact of what Israel did on civilians? Israel and the US celebrate the pager operation as a major achievement, calling it precise and targeted. But they are lying. They are liars, because really it was a terrorist attack, a war crime, because it also hit civilians. And you met tons of civilians, women and children, in your documentary. But in fact, this is not just my word; Human Rights Watch said it was a war crime. Booby-trapped pagers used by civilians on a daily basis—when they exploded, they didn’t target only Hezbollah fighters, because you know they are a part of Lebanese society, and they chose a peak time when families were gathered, when children came back from school. So when they exploded, they targeted, killed, and injured children, women, families, doctors, nurses. They are not all military; part of them are civilians. [Redwan Mortada:] And the injuries—I mean, just so people understand the injuries from this explosion. It exploded in people’s faces, so it was destroyed eyeballs, destroyed facial structure and bones, missing fingers. Really, really horrific stuff. I think you experienced—my colleague told me that when you wanted to give a neck mic to one of the children to start the interview, he ran away a bit because it was similar to the pager. [Rana:] No, they were scared. Yeah, the kids I spoke to were scared, of course. They have PTSD from this device because it looked similar. It’s just horrible. And the other thing, too, is people blinded. If you’re blind, you usually learn to read with your fingers, with Braille, but the pager—the way it exploded, people were holding it, so it also cut off people’s fingers in addition to taking away their sight, so they can’t even learn to read Braille. There are just so many layers of horror that this has impacted, and people are still getting surgeries two years later to fix their faces, if they can ever be fixed. It’s just horrifying and should not be celebrated. But you noted—and again, I encourage people to go watch the documentary because it goes into detail—Israel’s real aim was to have these exploding walkie-talkies kill as many as 20,000 fighters, and it didn’t manage to do that. So obviously they did a lot of damage to Hezbollah, but their ultimate operation failed. But connected to all this: yes, Hezbollah was able to demonstrate it survived, especially watching it fight in 2026. Like you mentioned, there weren’t major assassinations because Israel doesn’t even really know who’s in charge anymore, and they were able to fight the Israelis. However, Israel has managed to occupy a huge portion of Lebanon, and right now Hezbollah is not really responding to Israel’s daily attacks, killings, and bombings—it’s blown up like 60 villages at this point. So where does the battle stand today? Hezbollah has lost ground, Israel is expanding its occupation, and people are wondering why Hezbollah is not responding right now. What, in your opinion, is Hezbollah’s real capability as it stands today, and is there any deterrence left against Israeli aggression? [Redwan Mortada:] This question should be addressed to Hezbollah, but I will tell you my evaluation of how I’m looking at what’s going on now. In fact, the war did not finish yet. The war is still going on, and the war is not only in Lebanon—the war is in the region, the war between the United States of America and Iran, between Iran and Israel, between Hezbollah and Israel. We are part of this big war in this region. Until now, there are rules of engagement, and the last agreement is still going on, because if you can see in Lebanon, Israel doesn’t dare to target Beirut, to target the Beqaa, to target the Dahieh, because there are rules of engagement between the United States of America and Iran. I think we have to wait and see. During the past 15 months, if you remember, everyone went out and said Hezbollah is done, Hezbollah is finished. But when the battle erupted, we saw another equation on the ground. So I think we are still in the middle of the war; we cannot expect what will go on, whether there will be another round—and that’s what we think, there will be another round, the third round. And we hope that we can survive, we hope that we can kick the Israelis out of our country, because you know that they believe in their myth of Greater Israel, and they believe that and declared that they can take part of Lebanon and part of Syria to fulfill their dream and their myth. So we are fighting with these psychopaths who are now destroying our houses, destroying our lands, killing anyone in that yellow zone in the south of Lebanon. And the United States of America, unfortunately, is backing them and covering them, and our government is involved in this betraying. So let’s wait and see how things will go on. [Rana:] Well, Redwan, I want to thank you so much for this incredible two-part documentary that you put together. Again, we’ll include a link to it in the description for people to watch, and also for all of the incredible work you do. You really are one of the best journalists we have here in Lebanon. So thank you for all of the wonderful work you do, and hopefully we can have you on again soon. [Redwan Mortada:] Thank you. Thank you so much.

articles.title: Brazil bans online betting
articles.content: The impasse is over. After days of uncertainty over what Brazil should do about online betting, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government announced Friday in São Paulo that sports betting houses will be shut down nationwide. Online casinos, including gambling games such as Tigrinho , are banned as well. The bans on bets and online casinos took effect immediately. Lula is also expected to send Congress a bill establishing penalties for anyone who operates, runs, or promotes betting. The move came through a decree signed by Lula, which took effect right away. Finance Minister Dario Durigan made the announcement and explained the reasoning. “Our decision stems from the harmful effect that bets have had in Brazil,” Durigan said. He pointed to two moments of “shame and neglect” in how betting was handled under the previous governments of Michel Temer and Jair Bolsonaro. “First, Temer authorized bets and set a two-year deadline for regulation to prevent use by children and teenagers and to put measures in place against money laundering,” Durigan said. “Nothing was done, and the deadline was extended. But once again, nothing was done under Jair Bolsonaro’s government either.” Anyone who still has money in legal betting accounts will be able to withdraw it. “As of today, no more money can be deposited onto betting sites in Brazil,” Durigan said. “The sites will remain available until 11:59 p.m. on October 5 so that anyone with a balance in a betting account can withdraw their money.” After that, betting sites must forward the funds to banks through a special account set up for reimbursement, reporting the amount, the bettor’s individual taxpayer number, and the bank the bet came from. On October 6, all betting sites will be taken offline for good. Betting sites have been ordered to fully return the balances of bettors who still had money on their platforms between October 9 and 14. Starting October 14, the Caixa Econômica Federal Savings Bank will step in to help with reimbursements if bettors run into problems with other banks. The government also plans to step up enforcement now that all forms of betting are illegal. It will first coordinate with the telecommunications regulator Anatel to make sure all betting sites are taken offline. It will also track any new sites that appear after the ban. Any Pix or wire transfer for illegal betting, including bets or Tigrinho-style games, will also be banned. Bank accounts identified as belonging to betting sites or groups will be frozen, and the funds will be seized for use in public safety. The federal government’s FalaBR platform will also be used to receive reports of illegal betting. Durigan said the government will also launch a new version of its Desenrola debt relief program, this one focused on debts tied to betting. “Online gambling is closely linked to Brazilians’ debt problems. We’re going to build good credit alternatives and fight abusive lending,” Durigan said. “We will keep building a country free of bets, with more income for people and more opportunity to get back to a normal life.” The presidential decree will now go to Congress, which is in recess because of the elections. It will remain in effect for 60 days and can be extended for another 60. The government expects lawmakers to approve it in November, when they return to work. Health Minister Alexandre Padilha stressed the health concerns behind the government’s move to end sports betting and online casinos in Brazil. The problem goes beyond financial loss: gambling disorder is linked to anxiety, depression, loss of control, changes in sleep and mood, family conflict, isolation, damage to personal and professional relationships, and higher use of alcohol and other drugs. Data from the World Health Organization show that the suicide rate is 15 times higher among people with gambling disorder. Financial hardship is the main factor associated with suicide among bettors. The risk of developing an addiction is also three times higher among socioeconomically vulnerable people and 150% higher among online gamblers. In 2023, more than 28 million Brazilians had placed a bet in the previous 12 months, and 10.9 million showed risky or problematic gambling patterns. According to Padilha, the damage bets have caused to Brazil’s public health system (the SUS) comes to about $7.4 billion a year through suicide, lost quality of life due to depression, and the effects of job loss, eviction and incarceration. Among students, 20% have placed a bet at some point. “Between 2018 and 2025, visits to mental health clinics rose by 140%,” he said. Padilha also said women end up bearing a heavy impact even when they don’t bet themselves. “They often bet to try to save the finances of a son, a father, or a husband. Even when they don’t bet, they’re affected by rising violence, by increased drug use linked to the impact of betting, and by the decline in their family’s finances,” he said. “Women are the ones who bet the least, but they’re the ones who seek out the most support services for this problem,” Padilha said. Justice and Public Security Minister Wellington César Lima e Silva said Lula’s decision to end bets came after extensive discussions and consultations with experts from various fields. “This is a decision that protects, cares for and fights crime, all at once.” Lima e Silva noted that the betting industry is especially prone to money laundering and can create openings for organized crime. “We’re going to send a bill that creates five new criminal offenses to make sure the rules in this provisional measure are taken seriously across every segment,” he said. The new crimes planned include operating fixed-odds betting, even if authorized by a foreign authority (four to six years in prison); advertising fixed-odds betting or recruiting bettors (two to four years in prison and a fine); using personal data to recruit bettors (two to four years in prison and a fine, with a harsher sentence if the data involves betting history, health information, or belongs to a child or teenager); providing financial support for fixed-odds betting operations (two to four years in prison and a fine); and supplying an internet application for fixed-odds betting (two to four years in prison and a fine, with a harsher sentence if the app evades age or location verification or targets children or teenagers). In recent weeks, the government’s effort to impose tougher restrictions on bets ran into lobbying from the industry, aimed at soccer clubs and politicians. The presidential palace, the Planalto, began weighing the political and electoral impact of the measure, even as the president grew visibly moved by the toll betting debt has taken on Brazilians. On September 18, at a campaign event in Guarulhos, São Paulo, Lula responded to soccer clubs that had been pressuring the government to keep bets in place. “Today, soccer clubs, led by Corinthians and Flamengo, said that if bets end, soccer will end too,” Lula said. “São Paulo was world champion three times with no gambling company sponsor. Santos was world champion and had no gambling company sponsor. Flamengo was world champion and had no gambling company sponsor. My own Corinthians was world champion twice with no sponsorship from betting companies.” “This online gambling isn’t a game; it’s a disease. This bet business is the most horrifying thing I’ve seen in my life,” Lula continued. “I want you to know that, if it’s up to me, I will put an end to these bets.” An Atlas/Bloomberg poll released Wednesday found that 75% of Brazilians agree that online betting should be banned. According to the poll, 71% fully agree with banning bets and another 4% somewhat agree. In addition, 79% of Brazilians think advertising for online betting and bets should be restricted, and 88% disagree that online betting can be a way to supplement income. Support for banning bets is highest among women (79%), people who identify as left-wing (85%), people with a college education (77%) and residents of the Midwest (77%). articles.title: Lula and Trump Defend Opposing World Views at UN General Assembly
articles.content: The two main speeches at the opening of the U.N. General Assembly were delivered by Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and U.S. President Donald Trump. The leaders addressed many of the same issues, but their speeches offered sharply contrasting visions of the global order. Sérgio Costa, a sociology professor at the Free University of Berlin, described Lula’s speech as important and forceful, not only for its defense of multilateralism, but also for the statesmanship Lula displayed in his address. “I think Lula made this very clear: multilateralism is essential to global health, for example. Without multilateralism, we face vaccine shortages and the return of diseases that had been eradicated. Climate and the environment are multilateral issues. So is preventing wars, especially as we are living in a world experiencing a record number of conflicts. These are wars of territorial expansion, something we thought had been left behind in the 20th century, but which have returned with tremendous force,” Costa said during an interview on Conexão BdF, a program on Rádio Brasil de Fato. Trump, by contrast, offered few surprises as he defended U.S. interests and sought to place his country at the center of the world. “These are the imperialist interests of a power that has lost ground in the world and wants to regain it,” Costa said. The professor pointed to the document that guides U.S. national security policy, released at the end of last year. He said it explicitly lays out the goal of turning Latin America into a U.S. sphere of influence, with Brazil emerging as an obstacle to that effort. Trump adopted a belligerent tone. He spoke of annihilating Iran, made direct threats against Cuba and offered no mea culpa regarding Venezuela, acknowledging that the primary interest had always been the oil. “If we did not have leaders in different Latin American countries willing to hand over their wealth and national sovereignty to the United States, the strategy adopted by the U.S. would not work. It relies on elites that align themselves with this discourse of American hegemony, selling out their countries to build more power at home,” Costa said. For Costa, one possibility for changing this situation would be for Trump to suffer a defeat in the midterm elections. That could open the way for nations to strengthen the multipolar order on the world stage. “I believe it is possible to build multilateralism on the foundations that exist today,” said Costa. “In other words, even though these international organizations have been weakened, they have not disappeared.” Translated by: Panamerican Dispatch

articles.title: ‘Cut ties with Palantir’, say UK’s health workers
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: On Thursday, October 1, health workers, patients, and activists protested Palantir’s role in the National Health Service (NHS) at more than 40 locations across England. Their demonstrations were part of a global week of action demanding that governments cut ties with the spy-tech firm over human rights and privacy concerns. Rallies took place in front of Palantir’s London headquarters, as well as in Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle, Sheffield and many more cities. “Palantir’s tools are used by the Israeli military in Gaza and by ICE to track and surveil migrants in the US,” campaign groups – including Just Treatment, Health Workers for a Free Palestine, Medact, and Global Justice Now – stated . “A company profiting from human rights violations has no place in the NHS or in any of our public services.” Palantir’s track record opposes core health values Palantir currently holds a £330 million (approximately USD 436 million) NHS contract and has rolled out the service’s Federated Data Platform (FDP), managing sensitive patient data. The project has drawn criticism from virtually every group involved in the NHS: data workers say it lags behind local systems; patients share privacy and data ownership fears; and health workers insist Palantir’s record opposes the very values their profession embodies. “I cannot stay true to that [Hippocratic] oath and tolerate Palantir continuing to profit from, and grow its malign business model through an NHS contract,” said physician Rhiannon Osborne from Medact at Thursday’s rally. “Every pound we give them helps to legitimize and sustain human rights abuses and erosion of democratic rule of law across the world.” Read more: The global economic benefit from the genocide of Palestinians A central concern is the company’s support for Israel throughout the genocide in Gaza. “When we strive to save every possible life, they champion their ability to kill and celebrate their role in the repeated war crimes committed by Israel – including unprecedented deliberate attacks on the doctors, nurses, and paramedics I worked with,” pediatric neurologist Omar Abdel-Mannan stated. “No moral government should tolerate their involvement in our NHS or indeed any of our public services.” Campaigners repeated calls for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to end the contract as soon as possible. Under an exit clause in the original agreement, that moment could arrive as early as February 2027. Campaigners and several commissions are pressing the government to notify Palantir of its intention to withdraw ahead of this date. “The government only has two months to say no to Palantir and the momentum is all with us,” Good Law Project activists said at the rally in London. “All the energy is to say no to Palantir, say no to their global human rights abuses, say no to their crap technology that doesn’t work and get Palantir out of the NHS.” Unions back appeal to bar Palantir from public sector contracts Calls to break Palantir’s grip on public services resonate beyond Britain. On September 28, more than 120 groups and unions called upon European governments and the European Commission to “scrap all existing public sector contracts with the US tech company Palantir.” As reported by the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), the appeal seeks to end current agreements and bar the firm from future public contracts. It also urges governments to develop “alternative data solutions compatible with public service,” echoing NHS data workers’ recommendations. Read more: Palantir profits from European public services but avoids millions in taxes that fund them, new report shows “ Palantir’s ramping up of ‘war-related’ support for Israel during the genocide in Gaza and the apparent disdain of its leadership for democracy are just two clear signs that this company serves the interests of the rich and powerful, not the general public,” said Tim Bierley of Global Justice Now. “Yet it has been allowed to embed dubious technologies across our public services, giving it access to sensitive data and creating worrying new technical dependencies.” “The UK must work with other countries to end dependence on companies involved in human rights abuses, and end the outsourcing of the public sphere to a dangerous class of big tech oligarchs.” People’s Health Dispatch is a monthly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch . articles.title: Israel to divide central West Bank with settler-only highway
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: In late September, Israeli media reported that Netanyahu’s government intends to adjust access to key routes in the central West Bank. It plans to reopen Route 463 to settler-only traffic in the governorate of Ramallah and Al-Bireh. Yisrael Gantz , the leader of the Yesha Council (an umbrella organization representing Israeli municipal councils across Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the Jordan Valley) confirmed that plans to reopen the road received preliminary approval and funding. Preparations are also underway by the Israeli military to complete “the security, legal, and logistical” steps required to reopen the route (also known as Wallerstein Road). History of the road The road was paved in 1994 under the directions of Pinchas Wallerstein, a founder of the settlement movement, to connect the illegal settlements of Beit El (north-east of Ramallah and Al-Bireh) and Dolev (north-west of Jerusalem). However, following the outbreak of the Second Intifada in 2000, the Israeli army barred Israeli people from using the road for security reasons. They also placed a locked iron gate on its end near Ein Qiniya village, northwest of Ramallah. Why has the reopening of the route raised concerns among Palestinians in the West Bank? Experts argue that Israel’s move will impact not only the governorate itself, but the entire occupied West Bank because of its central location, major metropolitan status, and role as a commercial hub. To understand the repercussions of the route reopening, BreakThrough News spoke with Jamal Jumaa, a Palestinian activist, expert on Israeli settlement and apartheid-related issues, and coordinator of the Palestinian Grassroots Anti-Apartheid Wall Campaign (Stop the Wall). Aside from dividing the governorate’s northern and southern halves, Jumaa noted that reopening the road is dangerous because it will block the center of Ramallah and Al-Bireh from two-thirds of its villages, which are situated to the west. The prominent Palestinian activist added that when Israel builds such roads for settler traffic, it fences them off on both sides and prohibits the use of adjacent lands. The Israeli authorities consider those lands a buffer zone, citing the security of the settlers as their reason. “This entails setting up military towers and checkpoints. The road will cut off continuously inhabited Palestinian villages north-west and south-west of Ramallah. Therefore, we are talking about the establishment of roughly four military checkpoints along the road,” he continued. Jumaa pointed out that the road will complicate the life of Palestinians by restricting their access to vital healthcare and education facilities, including the Istishari Arab Hospital, Birzeit University, and the Arab American University. He also noted that the intended reopening of the road “is part of dividing and dividing more Palestinians from each other.” On the political level, Jumaa suggested that the road “hits the heart of the West Bank, which gives a clear signal to the Palestinian Authority that it has no sovereignty over anything.” It is worth noting that since its establishment, the Palestinian Authority has designated Ramallah and Al-Bireh as a de facto administrative capital. Yet, this has not prevented the Israeli authorities from fragmenting and isolating the governorate by establishing illegal settlements, military outposts, checkpoints, and gates.
